Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 1:

(p-2) Surat al-Mulk is Meccan, and it is also called al-Waqiyah (the Protector) and al-Munjiyah (the Deliverer), because it protects its reciter and delivers him from the punishment of the grave. Its verses number thirty.

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾. Barakah (blessing) means growth, increase and enlargement, whether sensory or intellectual, and also abundance of good and its permanence. Its attribution to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is according to the first meaning, which is the most fitting to the context, in view of His exaltedness above all else in His essence, attributes and acts. The form tabaraka (the reflexive form of the verb) is for intensification in this regard, for those forms that cannot conceivably be attributed to Him, such as takabbur (arrogance) and the like, are attributed to Him, glory be to Him, only in terms of their ends. According to the second meaning, it is in terms of the abundance of what overflows from Him upon His creatures of all kinds of goods. The form in that case may be used to indicate the growth and increase of those goods moment by moment, and instant by instant, according to their occurrence or the occurrence of their objects. And because it independently indicates the utmost perfection and announces the ultimate in magnificence, it is not permissible to use it of anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, nor to use other forms of it regarding Him, blessed and exalted be He. Its attribution to the relative pronoun (alladhi) is to cite what is in the relative clause as evidence for the realization of its content. The "hand" is a metaphor for complete power and perfect dominion, meaning: He is exalted and magnified in His essence above everything other than Him, in essence, attribute and act, the One in whose grip of power is the total disposal of all affairs.

﴿And He is over everything﴾ of things.

﴿Powerful﴾, exceedingly capable over it, disposing of it as His will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms. The sentence is conjoined to the relative clause, confirming its content and indicating that the rulings of His dominion, blessed and exalted be He, operate in grand matters and in their minutiae. And His saying, exalted be He:

The Quranic verse is: ﴿He who created death and life﴾. This begins an elaboration of some of the rulings of sovereignty and the effects of power, and an explanation that both are founded on the laws of wisdom and benefits, and lead to noble ends. The relative clause ﴿who created﴾ is a substitute for the first relative clause and is included with it in the testimony to His exaltedness, may He be exalted. According to our companions (the Ash'ari scholars), death is an existential attribute opposed to life. As for what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah, may He be exalted, created death in the form of a white-speckled black ram, which does not pass by anything or catch its scent without that thing dying, and created life in the form of a piebald mare, which does not pass by anything or catch its scent without that thing coming to life, this is a statement given in the manner of illustration and depiction. It has also been said that death is the absence of life, so that creating it then means determining it, or the removal of life. In any case, the closest view is that what is meant by death is the death that occurs (at a fixed time), and by life, what precedes and follows it, because of the evident connection between them to what the words of His, may He be exalted, express: ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. The seeking of the observation of these two for the goodness of deed is undoubtedly so, although the deed itself cannot be realized without worldly life. The mention of death first is because it is more conducive to the goodness of deed. The lam (of purpose) is connected to "created", meaning: He created your death and your life; and the alif and lam (in "the death" and "the life") are a substitute for the genitive complement, so that He may deal with you as one who tests you, which of you is best in deed, and then recompense you according to varying ranks in accordance with the varying levels of your knowledge and your deeds. For deed is not restricted to the deeds of the limbs. For this reason, the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him explained it with his saying: "Which of you has the best intellect, is the most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and the swiftest in obedience to Allah." For each of the heart and the body has a deed specific to it. Just as the first is nobler than the second, so too is the situation of their deeds. How could it not be so, when there is no deed without knowledge of Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, which is obligatory upon the servants and is the most excellent of all that is excellent? Its path is reflective, namely contemplation of the wondrous workmanship of Allah, may He be exalted, and pondering over His signs placed in the souls and the horizons. It has been narrated from him, Prayer and Peace be upon him, that he said: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta, for there was raised for him each day the like of the deeds of the people of the earth." They said: That was only the reflection on the matter of Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, which is necessarily the deed of the heart, since no one can by his limbs perform each day the like of the deeds of the people of the earth. The stating of the verb of trial, that is, its being followed by the interrogative particle, is not the well-known "suspension" which requires that the object not be mentioned at all, and which is specific to verbs of the heart, because it contains the meaning of knowledge with regard to its outcome, like "consider" and similar verbs. For this reason it has been treated as such by way of illustration. It has been said: by way of contingent metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya). The use of the comparative form, although the trial includes them all with regard to their deeds which are divided into the good and the better only, is to signal that what is intended in essence and as the primary purpose of the trial is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers, while the basic faith and obedience of the rest are also realized, due to the perfect mutual support of the factors that necessitate it. As for disregarding this, it is far from falling under the event, let alone being included in the series of the purpose of the divine acts. Rather, it is a deed that proceeds from its doer through his evil choice, without any justification or motive for it. In this there is, to a degree that is not hidden, encouragement to ascend to the heights of knowledge and the stages of acts of obedience, and a deterrent from engaging in their opposites. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the Overpowering, whom none who does evil escapes, ﴿the Forgiving﴾ to whoever of them repents.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 3:

﴿Who created seven heavens.﴾ It is said that it is a qualifier (*na't*) of "the Almighty, the Forgiving," or an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or a substitute (*badal*). The most apt view is that it is in the accusative, or in the nominative for praise (*al-madh*). It is connected in meaning to the two preceding relative clauses, although grammatically it is detached from them, as its detailed explanation was given earlier in the commentary on His words: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. It is included with them in the thread of witnessing through His exaltation toward Him, glory be to Him, and with the second relative clause in being a locus of trial, as His words express: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed.﴾

His words ﴿in layers﴾ (*tibaqan*) are a qualifier of "seven heavens," meaning "in agreement" (*mutabaqah*). It is a verbal noun (*masdar*), from "I fitted the sandal (*na'l*) when you patched it." It may be used as a qualifier of the passive participle, or its verbal noun is an emphasis for an omitted qualifier, meaning: they were made to fit one another in layers.

His words ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ are another qualifier of "seven heavens." Here the phrase "the creation of the Most Merciful" is placed in the position of a pronoun, for the sake of exalting it, and to indicate the cause of the ruling, and that He, exalted is He, created them by His overpowering power as mercy and bounty, and that in their origination there are magnificent blessings (p-4). Alternatively, it is a new sentence (*istina'*), and the address is to the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The "min" (from) is for emphasizing the negation, meaning: you see in it no discrepancy at all, that is, no difference and no lack of proportion, from *al-fawt* (failing to reach), since each of two things that are mismatched lacks some of what the other has. It is also read *min tafawwut*, and the two have the same meaning.

His words ﴿So turn your sight back; do you see any cracks?﴾ are connected to what precedes in the sense of causation (*tasbib*): He first informed that there is no discrepancy in their creation, then it was said: "Turn your sight back," until this becomes clear to you by direct observation, and no doubt whatsoever remains with you. *Al-futur* means fissures and rifts, the plural of *fitr*, which is a crack. It is said: "He split it, and it split apart" (*fatarahu fa-infatara*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 4:

﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ That is: two further returns in searching for a flaw. The dual here is used to mean repetition and multiplicity, as in "labbayka" and "sa'dayka" (expressions of repeated, ready response), meaning: return after return, however many times. ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled﴾ That is: far off, deprived of reaching whatever fault or defect it sought, as though it were driven away from that with abasement and humiliation. ﴿while it is fatigued﴾ That is: weary, from the long repetition and the frequent reviewing. And the words of the Exalted:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 5:**

﴿And We have indeed adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. This is an explanation that the creation of the heavens is in the utmost beauty and splendour, following the explanation of their being free of any flaw or defect. The opening of the sentence with an oath serves to show the complete concern with its content; that is, "By God, We have indeed adorned the nearest of the heavens to the earth ﴿with lamps﴾," i.e., with shining stars (kawakib) that give light at night like the light of lamps (suruj), among the wandering stars (sayyarat) and the fixed stars (thawabit). They appear as though all of them were fixed in it, although some of them are in the other heavens. This is only because each one of them is created in a pattern of such delicacy that thoughts are bewildered in understanding it, and in a form of such excellence that gazes are lost in perceiving it.

﴿And We have made them missiles for the devils﴾. We have given them another benefit, which is the stoning of your enemies by the striking down of meteors (shuhub) kindled from the fire of the stars. It has also been said that the meaning is: We have made them conjectures and stonings concerning the unseen for the devils of mankind, namely the astrologers (munajjimun). The context does not support this interpretation. The word rujum (missiles) is the plural of rajm, with a fatha on the ra', and it is that by which something is stoned.

﴿And We have prepared for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾, after being burned in this world by the meteors.

And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Jahannam (Hell), [this refers to] the devils and others. And it was recited with the accusative (naṣb) on the basis that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the punishment of the blaze" (ʿadhāb al-saʿīr). And "for those who disbelieve" is [governed] by "for them" [in the preceding verse]. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, i.e., Jahannam.

﴿When they are cast into it, they hear for it﴾. That is, for Hell. The phrase *lahā* is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the word *shahīqan* in the verse ﴿a roaring (*shahīqan*)﴾. This is because it was originally a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of that word, and when it was placed first it became a *ḥāl*. The sense is: they hear it, being for it (*kā'inan lahā*) a *shahīq*, that is, a sound like the braying of donkeys, namely its dreadful, hideous roar. They said: the *shahīq* is in the chest, and the *zafīr* is in the throat. ﴿And it boils up with them﴾. That is, and the situation is that it seethes with them like the seething of a cauldron with what is in it. Attributing the *shahīq* to its inhabitants, both from among them and from among those who were cast into it before them, is like the verse ﴿For them therein is a *zafīr* and a *shahīq*﴾. It is refuted by the verse of Allah, the Exalted, which says:

(p-5) ﴿تَكادُ تَمَيَّزُ﴾ means: it nearly splits apart and separates into pieces, ﴿مِنَ الغَيْظِ﴾, that is, from the intensity of wrath against them. This is explicit that it is one of the effects of anger against them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿سَمِعُوا لَها تَغَيُّظًا وزَفِيرًا﴾ [They hear from it a raging and a roaring]. How does this compare with their wailing (shahiq), which arises from the intensity of the painful torment they suffer? The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "تَفُورُ" (it boils over), or another predicate (khabar). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿كُلَّما أُلْقِيَ فِيها فَوْجٌ﴾ [Whenever a group is thrown into it] is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to explain the condition of its inhabitants after explaining the condition of the Fire itself. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause referring to its pronoun, meaning: whenever a company of disbelievers is cast into it. ﴿سَألَهم خَزَنَتُها﴾ [its keepers ask them], by way of rebuke and reproach, so that they may increase in torment upon torment and in regret upon regret. ﴿ألَمْ يَأْتِكم نَذِيرٌ﴾ [Did no warner come to you?] — one who recites to you the signs of your Lord and warns you of the meeting of this your Day, as occurred in Surat al-Zumar, and their answer also expresses this.

﴿They said﴾, acknowledging that He, the Exalted, had completely removed their excuses. ﴿Yes, indeed a warner came to us﴾, combining the particle of response with the very sentence being answered; this is for the sake of emphasizing their admission of the warner's coming, and as an expression of regret over the happiness they missed by not believing, and as a preparation for explaining the negligence that they committed, in remorse and grief over it. That is: each group of those multitudes said, "A warner has come to us," meaning one warner in reality, or one in legal standing, like the prophets of the Children of Israel, for they were legally considered one warner, who warned us and recited to us what God, the Exalted, had sent down to him of His signs. ﴿So we denied﴾ that warner in his being a warner from Him, the Exalted. ﴿And we said﴾, concerning what he recited of the signs, in excess of denial and persistence in rejection: ﴿God has not sent down﴾ to anyone ﴿anything﴾ of things, let alone the sending down of signs to you. ﴿You are not﴾, that is, you are not, in your claim that He, the Exalted, sent down to you signs by which you warn us, ﴿except in great error﴾, far from truth and rightness. The use of the plural pronoun of address, although each group's addressee is its own warner, is to give precedence to him over his like, in emphasis of denial and persistence in misguidance, as is indicated by the generalization of "what was sent down" while omitting mention of the one to whom it was sent, for it is necessarily hinted at by its generality. As for making the denial of one the same as the denial of all, this is a real matter to which recourse is had to magnify the crimes they committed; there is no room for considering it from their side, nor for including it under their expression. How could it be otherwise? For it depends on considering the ijma' (consensus) of the warners on what does not differ among the laws and rulings by the differences of eras and years. And where are they from that? The choking has come between them and the poem (i.e., they were unable to articulate it). This is when what has been mentioned is taken as a report about each one of the groups. As for when it is taken as a report about all of them, then "warner" is either in the sense of the plural, because it is of the pattern fa'il, or a verbal noun estimated with a general genitive construct, that is, "people of a warner," or a qualifier, so that both sides of the address agree in plurality. Whoever considers plurality by one of the three aspects under the first assumption, and does not restrict its consideration to the last assumption, has confused the matters, and doubts have mixed up in him. It has also been permitted that the address is from the speech of the guardians (khazana) of Hell to the disbelievers, with the intention of saying; and that their meaning by "error" is what they were upon in the world, or their destruction, or the punishment of their error, calling it by the name of its cause. And it may be that it is from the speech of the messengers to the disbelievers, and they have referred it to the guardians. So reflect, and be upon the manifest truth.

Also they say, admitting that they were not among those who listen or reason: ﴿Had we been listening﴾ to speech, ﴿or reasoning﴾ about anything, ﴿we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze﴾. That is, we would not have been counted among them or among their followers, and they are the devils, in keeping with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾. It is as if the guardians of Hell said to them, amid the rebuke: "Did you not hear the signs of your Lord, and did you not reason about their meanings, so that you would not deny them?" And they answered with this.

﴿So they confessed their sin﴾, which is their disbelief and their denial of the signs of Allah and His messengers. ﴿Fa-suḥqan﴾ (so, away with them, far removed) is read with a sukun on the ḥā’, and it is also read with a ḍammah. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used for emphasis (mu’akkid). It may be for a transitive verb derived from the augmented form, with the augmentations removed, as in the expression “qi‘dak Allah” (Allah keep you sitting), meaning: “So Allah made them far away (fa-asḥaqahumu Allah), that is, He removed them from His mercy with a distancing (suḥqan), that is, an act of removal (isḥāqan).” Or it may be for a verb that follows from that verb, meaning: “So Allah removed them, and so they were removed (fa-suḥiqū), that is, they were distanced with a distancing (suḥqan), that is, remoteness (bu‘dan),” as in the words of the one who said:

*“And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of the wealth only what is scraped away or stripped bare.”*

That is, time left nothing, so nothing remained except the scraped-away and the stripped-bare. This is the meaning of his words: “…and so on.” On both of these readings, the words of the Most High, ﴿And He caused it to grow as a good growth﴾, are also explained. The lām in His words, ﴿for the companions of the Blaze﴾, is for clarification (lil-bayān), as in “hayta laka” (come, I am ready for you) and similar expressions. By them is meant the devils and those who are counted among them by way of taghlīb (giving precedence to the dominant group, a rhetorical device in which one category is used to include another).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen, for them there is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ That is: they fear His punishment while it is absent from them, or while they are absent from it, or [they fear it] away from the sight of people, or [it means] with what is hidden from them, which is their hearts. ﴿For them there is forgiveness﴾ great for their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 13:

﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it aloud﴾ is an explanation of the equal standing of secret and open speech with respect to His knowledge, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿Whether one of you conceals speech or openly declares it, it is the same﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It was revealed concerning the polytheists, who used to malign the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and revelation would come to him, peace and blessings be upon him. Some of them said to others: "Keep your speech secret, lest the Lord of Muhammad hear." So it was said to them: "Whether you keep it secret or declare it aloud, indeed Allah knows it." The mention of the secret before the open is to announce their exposure and the occurrence of what they were wary of from the outset, and to emphasize the comprehensiveness of His all-encompassing knowledge of all things known, as if His knowledge of what they keep secret were more capable than His knowledge of what they declare aloud, although in reality the two are on an equal footing. This is because the knowledge of the Exalted regarding His objects of knowledge is not by way of the acquisition of their forms; rather, the existence of each thing in itself is knowledge with respect to Him, exalted is He. Or it is because the level of the secret precedes the level of the open, for there is nothing declared aloud except that it, or its beginnings, is hidden in the heart, to which secrecy usually attaches. Thus His knowledge's attachment to its first state precedes its attachment to its second state.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ is a reason for what precedes it and a confirmation of it. In the form of the intensive adjective (fa'il), in the definite article of totality (lam al-istighraq) on "al-sudur" (the breasts), and in describing the inner thoughts by their possession (of the breasts), there is an eloquence beyond which there is no further degree. It is as if it were said: He is exceedingly thorough in encompassing the hidden thoughts of all people and their concealed secrets lodged in their breasts, to the extent that they scarcely ever leave them at all. How then could what you keep secret and what you declare aloud be hidden from Him?! It is also permissible that by "dhat al-sudur" (what is within the breasts) is meant the hearts that are in the chest, and the meaning is: He is Knowing of the hearts and their states, so no secret of their secrets is hidden from Him. His saying, exalted is He:

Does He who created not know? This is a denial and negation of any lack in the encompassing of His knowledge, exalted is He, over what is concealed and what is manifest. That is, does not the One who brought into existence all things, in accordance with the requirement of His wisdom, of which the concealed and the manifest are part, know the secret and the open?

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of "*yaʿlamu*" (He knows). It reinforces the denial and negation. That is, does He not know that, while His knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden within it?

It is permissible for "*man khalaqa*" (who created) to be in the accusative, so that the meaning is: Does Allah not know whom He created, while He is of this standing in the all-encompassing reach of knowledge? There is no justification for leaving knowledge without an object by treating it like "*yuʿṭī wa-yamnaʿu*" (He gives and withholds), in the sense of "Would not the one who created be knowing?" This is because creation is not possible without knowledge, and the circumstantial clause would then be devoid of benefit. The structure of the speech would then be: "Would He not be knowing," while He is one who is emphatic in knowledge.

He it is who made the earth subservient to you (ﷺ no) — "made the earth docile (dhalul) for you, easy for you to traverse. The placing of "for you" (lakum) before the two objects of "made" (ja'ala), although its proper place is after them, is for emphasis on what has been fronted and to create anticipation for what has been delayed. For what should be first, when it is delayed, especially when the fronted element indicates that the delayed element is among the benefits for the addressees, the soul remains awaiting its arrival, so that when it is mentioned it settles in the soul with greater firmness.

The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So walk in its broad paths﴾ indicates the ordering of the command upon the aforementioned making. That is: traverse its sides or its mountains. This is a metaphor for the extreme of making it docile, for the shoulder (mankib) of a camel is the thinnest of its limbs and the least able to bear a rider stepping on it with his foot. So when He has made the earth so subdued that walking upon its shoulders becomes possible, nothing of it remains that has not been made docile.

﴿And eat of His provision﴾, that is, seek out the bounties of God, exalted is He. ﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾, that is, the return after the resurrection, not to any other, so exert yourselves in thanking Him for His blessings and favours.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 16:

﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven﴾ That is: the angels entrusted with managing this world; or God, glory be to Him, according to the interpretation that "He who is in the heaven" means His command and His decree; or according to the assumption of the Arabs, since they used to suppose that He, exalted is He, is in the heaven. That is: Are you secure from the One whom you suppose to be in the heaven, while He is exalted above place? ﴿that He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾ after He had made it subservient for you, so that you walk through its broad paths and eat of His provision, because of your ingratitude for that blessing. That is: He would turn it over upon you, so that it engulfs you within it, as He did with Qarun. The phrase "that He will cause the earth to swallow you" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "He who is in the heaven." It was also said that it is by omission of the preposition, meaning: from that He would cause the earth to swallow you. ﴿Then behold, it shakes﴾ That is: it trembles, moving back and forth, contrary to the state of submission and tranquility it had been in.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 17:

﴿Or do you feel secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send against you a hurricane of stones?﴾ This is a turning away (idrab, a shift) from the threat mentioned before, and a transition to threatening in another way. That is: rather, do you feel secure from He who is in the heaven ﴿that He will send against you a hāṣib (a hurricane of stones)﴾, i.e., stones from the sky, as He sent them against the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant. It has also been said: a wind containing stones and pebbles, as if it uproots the pebbles because of its severity and strength. And it has been said: it is a cloud containing stones. ﴿Then you will surely know﴾ soon, without doubt, ﴿how was My warning (nadhir)﴾, i.e., My warning when you witness what you were warned of. But knowledge will not benefit you at that time. It was also read: (fasa-ya'lamūn), with the ya' (third person).

And indeed, those before them denied. That is, before the disbelievers of Mecca, from among the disbelievers of the earlier nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, and their likes. The shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) serves to display (li-ibraz) aversion from them. "So how was My denunciation (nakir)?" That is, My rejection of them by sending down punishment; that is, it was of the utmost terror and horror. This is the locus of the emphatic oath (mawrid al-ta'kid al-qasami), not merely their denial. And in it there is an extent of emphasis in consoling the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in intensifying the warning to his people that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 19:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ — i.e., they were heedless and did not reflect — ﴿the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them in?﴾ — spreading their wings (ṣāffāt, "in rows") in the air while flying. For when they spread them, they align their primary feathers in a row (ṣaffan). ﴿And folding them in﴾ (yaqbiḍna) — drawing them together when they strike them against their sides at times and at other times, to gain support from them for movement. This is the secret behind preferring "yaqbiḍna," which indicates the repeated occurrence of folding, time after time, over "qābiḍāt" (folding in). ﴿None holds them up﴾ in the air during spreading and folding, contrary to what their nature would require, ﴿except the Most Merciful﴾, whose mercy encompasses everything, by creating them in forms and characteristics and preparing them to glide through the air. The clause is either a new sentence or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in yaqbiḍna. ﴿Indeed He is All-Seeing of everything﴾, knowing how the originated things are originated and how the created things are managed. And His Exalted saying:

﴿Who is this, the one who is an army for you to help you apart from the Most Merciful?﴾ This is a rebuke to them by denying that they have any helper other than God, Exalted is He, as the mention of the title "the Most Merciful" hints and as His saying supports: "None holds them up except the Most Merciful." Or (the meaning is) a helper against His punishment, Exalted is He, which is the more fitting reading in light of what follows, His saying: ﴿If He withholds His provision﴾. It is like His saying: ﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾, in both meanings together, except that the interrogation there is directed at the preventer itself and whether it exists, while here it is directed at identifying the helper, in order to rebuke them by showing their inability to identify him. The "am" (disjunctive "am", meaning "or rather") is a presumed disjunctive particle, equivalent to "bal" (rather), which indicates a shift from rebuking them for neglecting to reflect on what they witness of the states of birds, which point to the wondrous effects of the power of God, Mighty and Majestic, to the rebuke with what has been mentioned. The shift to direct address is for emphasis in this matter. There is no way to presume the interrogative hamza (أ) with it, because what follows it is "man" (مَن), the interrogative, which is the subject (مبتدأ), and "hadha" (هذا) is its predicate, and the relative pronoun with its clause is its attribute, as in His saying: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him?﴾. The choice of "hadha" is to belittle the one being pointed to. "Yansurukum" (يَنْصُرُكُمْ) is an attribute of "jund" (جند) according to its wording. As for ﴿apart from the Most Merciful﴾, according to the first reading it is either a circumstantial phrase (حال) from the doer of "yansurukum", or a qualifier of its verbal noun; according to the second reading it is connected to "yansurukum", as in His saying: ﴿Who will help me against God?﴾. So the meaning is: "Rather, who is this insignificant one who, in your claim, is an army for you that helps you with help apart from His help, Exalted is He, or helps you against a punishment coming from God, Mighty and Majestic." The supposition that "am" is equivalent (معادلة) to His saying: ﴿Have they not seen...﴾ and so on, together with the claim that "man" is interrogative, is something with no closeness to it at all. His saying: ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ is a parenthetical clause (اعتراض) that confirms what precedes it, censuring them for the utmost misguidance they are in, meaning: they think they are protected from calamities by the protection of their gods, not by His protection alone; or their gods protect them from the might of God only in great delusion and gross misguidance from the side of Satan, having in that nothing of any worth at all. The shift to the third person is to indicate that their state calls for turning away from them and for making their ugliness known to others. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to condemn them for disbelief and to explain the cause of their delusion by it. The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 21:

﴿Or who is it that provides for you if He withholds His provision?﴾ That is: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿His provision﴾ by withholding the rain and all its origins, as has been detailed earlier. Except that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, they have persisted in arrogance and aversion﴾ indicates an omitted element which the context calls for, as if it were said: after the complete rebuke and the demonstration of their incapacity, they were not affected by that and did not submit to the truth; rather they persisted and continued in arrogance (*'utuw*), that is, obstinacy, haughtiness, transgression, and aversion (*nufur*), that is, fleeing away from the truth. And His saying, may He be exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 22:

﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ ... etc. It is a parable struck for the polytheist and the monotheist, clarifying their respective states and establishing the reality of their two ways. The fa' (the "fa" particle, indicating sequence) orders this on what has appeared of their evil condition, their falling into the pits of delusion, their mounting the back of the blind beast of arrogance and aversion, and their failure to be guided, in the course of argument, to any direction in which some measure of rectitude might be imagined. For the placing of the hamza (the interrogative particle, i'rab-wise a question marker) before it is merely formal, owing to its requirement of initial position; as for the meaning, the matter is the reverse, as is well known. Indeed, even if "hal" (another interrogative particle) were in the place of the hamza, it would be said: "Hal man yamshi mukibban..." etc. Al-mukibb is one who has fallen upon his face. It is said: akabba, meaning he fell upon his face; its real sense is: he became one who has a fall, and he entered into the kabb, as in "aqshaʿa al-ghamam" (the clouds cleared), meaning: it became possessed of clearing. The meaning is: Is one who walks while stumbling at every moment, and falling upon his face at every step, because of the roughness of his path and the disorder of his faculties, more guided to the goal he intends, [than] ﴿one who walks upright﴾, that is, standing, safe from staggering and stumbling, ﴿on a straight path﴾, its parts level, with no crookedness in it and no deviation. It has been said: the predicate of the second clause is omitted, being indicated by the predicate of the first; but there is no need for that, since the second is coordinated with the first as a coordination of single term with single term, like your saying: "Is Zayd the more excellent, or ʿAmr?" It has also been said: by the one who walks prone is meant the blind, and by the upright one the seeing. It has also been said: the one who walks prone is the one who will be gathered upon his face into the Fire, and the one who walks upright is the one who will be gathered on his feet into the Garden.

Say: "It is He Who brought you into being" (originating you in a wondrous creation), "and made for you hearing" (so that you hear the verses of Allah and act upon the commands and prohibitions within them, and take admonition from their exhortations), "and sight" (so that you look with them at the cosmic signs bearing witness to the affairs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic), "and hearts" (af'idah, plural of fu'ad; so that you reflect with them on what you hear and see of the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanzihiyyah) and the cosmic signs, and ascend the ladders of faith and obedience), "little is it that you give thanks."

That is, by using them for the purposes for which they were created, namely the matters mentioned. "Qalilan" (little) is an adjective of an omitted noun, and "ma" is redundant (za'idah), for emphasis on paucity; meaning: "little thanks" you give, or you give thanks "for a little time." It has also been said that "qillah" (paucity) here expresses non-existence.

Say: "It is He who created you and multiplied you upon the earth," that is, He alone created you and caused you to increase in it, not other than Him. ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾ for recompense, not to anything else, whether as a partner or independently; so build your affairs upon that.

And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled?" — out of the extreme of their arrogance and obstinacy — ﴿When will this promise be fulfilled?﴾ That is, the promised resurrection (al-hashr), as indicated by His saying, "And to Him you will be gathered" (Qur'an 67:24). ﴿If you are truthful﴾ — they address it to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, since they were sharing with him, peace and blessings be upon him, in the promise and in reciting the verses that contain it. The response to the conditional is omitted, meaning: "If you are truthful in what you tell us about the coming of the Hour and the resurrection, then specify its time."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 26:

﴿Say: The knowledge [of it] is only with Allah﴾, that is: the knowledge of its time is with Allah, mighty and majestic; He does not reveal it to anyone other than Him, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾.

﴿And I am only a clear warner﴾: I warn you of the certain occurrence of what has been promised. As for the knowledge of the time of its occurrence, it is not among the functions of warning. The fa' in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْهُ﴾ is a *fasihah* (an elliptical particle, one that signals omitted words) that points to the implied presence of two clauses, and the conditional sentence is ordered after them. It is as if it were said: "The promised thing had come to them, and they saw it. So when they saw it..." and so on, as its verification was discussed earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَلَمّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا عِنْدَهُ﴾ ("When he saw it settled beside him"). However, the implied element there is a fact that has occurred, linked to what precedes it by the *fa* (the particle of sequence). Here, by contrast, it is something treated as though it has occurred, coming in the manner of a resumption (*isti'naf*).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿زُلْفَةً﴾ ("near") is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) of the object of "رَأوْا" ("they saw"). It may be so either by supposing an omitted noun, meaning "possessing nearness and proximity," or because it is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle, meaning "drawing near," or because it is a verbal noun described by it for emphasis, or because it is an adverb of place, meaning "they saw it in a place of nearness."

﴿سِيئَتْ وُجُوهُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed"): this is because gloom has overtaken them and dust and humiliation have covered them. The placing of the relative pronoun in the position of their pronoun serves to censure them for disbelief and to give the reason for their distress.

﴿وَقِيلَ﴾ ("and it will be said") is for rebuke to them and to intensify their punishment.

﴿وَقِيلَ هَذا الَّذِي كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَدَّعُونَ﴾ ("and it will be said: This is what you used to call for"), meaning: what you seek in the world and ask to hasten, in denial and mockery, on the basis that "تَفْتَعِلُونَ" (*taftaʿilūn*, "you call for") is derived from *duʿāʾ* (calling/supplication). It has also been said that it is derived from *daʿwā* (claim), meaning: you claim that there is no resurrection and no gathering. It has been read as (تَدْعُونَ هَذا) (*tadʿūna hadhā*). It has been narrated from Mujahid that the promised thing was the punishment of the Day of Badr, but this is far-fetched.

Say: "Tell me: if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy on us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"

(Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim)

"Tell me" (أيْ: أخْبِرُونِي): that is, inform me.

"If Allah destroys me" (إنْ أهْلَكَنِيَ اللَّهُ): that is, causes me to die. The expression "destroys" (الإهلاك, al-ihlak) is used for death because the disbelievers used to invoke destruction (الهلاك) upon the Prophet ﷺ and upon the believers.

"And those with me" (وَمَن مَعِيَ): that is, the believers.

"Or has mercy on us" (أوْ رَحِمَنا): by postponing our terms (آجالنا). So we are within the protection of His mercy, awaiting one of the two good outcomes (لإحدى الحسنيين).

"Who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?" (فَمَن يُجِيرُ الكافِرِينَ مِن عَذابٍ ألِيمٍ): that is, no one will save you from it, whether we die or remain alive. The placing of "the disbelievers" (الكافرين) in the position of their pronoun (ضميرهم) serves to record disbelief against them and to give the reason for the negation of deliverance by it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 29:

﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾ — i.e., He whom I call you to worship is the Lord (mawla) of all blessings. ﴿We have believed in Him﴾ alone, for we know that everything other than Him is either a blessing or one who is blessed.

﴿And upon Him we have relied﴾ — not upon anyone else at all, for we know that whatever else exists, whatever it may be, is utterly powerless (bi-ma'zil) to benefit or harm.

﴿So you will soon know﴾ — definitely and without delay ﴿who it is that is in clear error﴾ — whether we or you. It is also read (qurida) as ﴿fasa-yaʿlamun﴾ with the yaʾ (ya' tahtaniyya, the letter of the third person masculine plural).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 67, verse 30:

﴿Say: Tell me﴾, i.e., inform me, ﴿if your water should become sunken﴾, i.e., sunk completely into the earth. It has also been said: to the point that buckets cannot reach it. The word (ghawr) is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective.

﴿Then who will bring you clear water?﴾ Flowing, or apparent and easily accessible. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Mulk, it is as if he has enlivened the Night of Qadr."
